To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) there is a large ethnic difference in reported GP–patient interpersonal communication; (2) this difference is concentrated in older women from South Asian ethnic groups; and (3) younger patients who described their ethnicity in the survey as ‘Any other White’ had particularly negative experiences of GP–patient interpersonal care.
there are large differences in the quality of doctor–patient communications between patients of different ethnic groups, which are concentrated in particular age and gender subgroups.
the effect of a patient’s ethnicity on reported doctor-patient communication varied by both gender and age.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the relationship between ethnicity, age and gender in determining the quality of doctor–patient relationships, as reported in a national survey of patients in primary care.
the quality of doctor–patient relationships in primary care, as measured by the English General Practice Patient Survey.
how reported GP– patient communication differs between patients from different minority ethnic groups, and how these differences vary between age and gender groups.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is a significant difference between the ethnic groups and the age groups in terms of the quality of doctor–patient communications.

the effect of ethnic background on reported GP–Patient communication varies by age and gender, and that the effect is particularly marked for older female Asian and younger ‘Any Other White’ patients.

the differences in the quality of doctor–patient interaction between white and non-white ethnic groups in England vary by age and gender, with the most negative experiences reported by older female Asian patients.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
there are significant ethnic differences in reported GP–patient communications.
there is a significant difference in doctor–patient communication between white British and minority ethnic groups in England and that this difference varies by age and gender.
the effect of patient ethnicity on GP–patient communication depends on both age and gender.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the differences in experience of doctor–patient interactions between white British and minority ethnic groups are not universal, and vary by age and gender in ways that have not previously been documented.
there are marked differences in experience between different ethnic groups, and that these differences are concentrated in particular age and gender groups.
the effect of ethnic background on doctor–patient communications is not uniform across the population.
